title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 68 (Power of company to purchase its own securities)

content.overview: Section 68 allows buy-back of own shares or specified securities if articles authorise it and the source, cap, solvency and process conditions are met.
content.glance: Section 68 allows buy-back of own shares or specified securities if articles authorise it and the source, cap, solvency and process conditions are met.
content.study: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 68 (Power of company to purchase its own securities). Buy-back may be funded from free reserves, the securities premium account or proceeds of an issue of other shares or specified securities, but not proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind. The articles must authorise the buy-back. A special resolution is generally required; the statutory exception permits a Board resolution for a buy-back within the 10% band specified in section 68(2). The aggregate buy-back limit is 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves, with a separate 25% of paid-up equity capital limit for equity shares in a financial year. Securities must be fully paid, and the post-buy-back debt-equity ratio must not exceed 2:1 unless a notified exception applies. Section 68 also prescribes solvency declaration, completion, extinguishment, restrictions on further issue, records and returns. Listed companies must comply with applicable SEBI regulations. Section 70 imposes additional prohibitions, including the three-year post-cure rule for specified defaults and compliance with sections 92, 123, 127 and 129. Check the current Act, rules and applicable listed-company regulations before relying on procedural deadlines or exceptions.

sections.heading: Authority and funding sources
sections.body: The articles must authorise the buy-back. Permitted sources are free reserves, the securities premium account or proceeds of an issue of other shares or specified securities. Proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or securities cannot fund the buy-back.

sections.heading: Resolution and quantitative limits
sections.body: A special resolution is generally required. The section's exception permits a Board resolution for a buy-back within the specified 10% band. The aggregate cap is 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves; buy-back of equity shares is separately capped at 25% of paid-up equity capital in a financial year.

sections.heading: Fully paid securities and debt-equity ratio
sections.body: The shares or other specified securities must be fully paid. The post-buy-back debt-equity ratio must not exceed 2:1 unless the Central Government has prescribed an exception for a class of companies.

sections.heading: Solvency, completion and extinguishment
sections.body: Section 68 prescribes a declaration of solvency and process requirements. The buy-back must be completed within the statutory period and the bought-back securities extinguished/destroyed within the prescribed period. Verify the current statutory text and rules for exact filing, timing and dematerialised-security requirements.

sections.heading: Further issue, records and return
sections.body: Section 68 restricts further issue of the same kind of shares or specified securities after buy-back, subject to statutory exceptions, and requires prescribed records and a return within the statutory deadline. Verify current rule/SEBI requirements for the particular company and transaction.

sections.heading: Additional prohibition under section 70
sections.body: Section 70 applies additional prohibitions: specified indirect purchase routes, certain repayment/dividend/loan defaults unless cured and three years have elapsed, and non-compliance with sections 92, 123, 127 and 129.

provisions.title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 68: Power of company to purchase its own securities

examples.title: Same-kind proceeds
examples.body: Buy-back of equity funded by a fresh equity issue is not a permitted source.

examples.title: Default bar
examples.body: An uncured deposit default attracts the s. 70 prohibition.

hypotheticals.question: A company proposes to fund a buy-back using proceeds of a fresh issue of the same kind of shares. Is that a permitted source?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 68 excludes proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or specified securities.

hypotheticals.question: A company meets section 68's resolution and funding requirements but has not complied with section 129. Can it proceed?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 70(2) separately bars buy-back where the company has not complied with section 129. Section 68 compliance does not remove section 70 prohibitions.

distinctions.title: Section 68 buy-back power and section 70 prohibitions
distinctions.left: Section 68 states the general power, funding sources and procedural/quantitative conditions.
distinctions.right: Section 70 imposes additional bars that can prohibit a buy-back despite section 68 compliance.

misconceptions.trap: Treating the 25% aggregate cap and the equity-share financial-year cap as the same test.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the aggregate paid-up capital/free-reserves cap and the separate equity-share cap independently.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming a Board resolution is sufficient for every buy-back.
misconceptions.correction: A special resolution is generally required; the Board-resolution exception applies only within the statutory 10% band.

misconceptions.trap: Checking section 68 alone and ignoring section 70.
misconceptions.correction: Section 70 adds prohibitions, including the three-year post-cure rule and section 92/123/127/129 compliance.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Can a company hold bought-back shares as treasury stock?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: No. The buy-back scheme requires extinguishment and physical destruction or demat equivalent within the prescribed period, not a treasury holding.
